title: International Proceedings
subtitle: Where the case stands before Serbia, Interpol, the UN and the ECHR.
intro: International institutions are engaged here as independent verification forums — not as a form of pressure, but as the mechanism international law exists to provide when domestic processes fall short. Each institution examines a distinct aspect of the same set of facts.

items.status: Final stage — decision now with the Minister of Justice
items.text: After the Belgrade Court of Appeal confirmed that the conditions for extradition are met, the file passed to the Minister of Justice — the final step in this procedure, with no further avenue of appeal available. At this stage the minister has the discretion to refuse extradition if the request appears to be politically or commercially motivated, or if there is a credible risk to the person's human rights.
items.focus: In practice, Serbian ministers of justice very rarely refuse extradition once the courts have found formal grounds to be satisfied. This is precisely why parallel engagement with international mechanisms is the only realistic means of bringing external scrutiny to bear on this decision.

items.status: 🔄 Under review — CCF confirmed receipt on 28 October 2025
items.text: Russia activated an international wanted notice through a Red Notice issued on 25 January 2025, based on an in-absentia arrest warrant issued by the Tversky District Court of Moscow on 27 December 2024. The defence challenged the notice by filing a complaint with the Interpol Commission for the Control of Files (CCF) — the only body authorised to review the legal basis of notices and order their removal. On 28 October 2025 the CCF formally notified the defence that a review had begun (ref. CCF/135/R1610.25) and asked for any further materials within one month.
items.focus: The central argument rests on Article 3 of the Interpol Constitution, which expressly prohibits the organisation from involvement in matters of a commercial nature. The transaction at the heart of the charge has been found lawful by arbitration courts through to the Russian Supreme Court — this is the key evidence that the dispute is commercial, not criminal. There is a further argument: the Red Notice itself describes Lagovsky as an 'enterprise engineer', which directly contradicts his documented status as a self-employed independent lawyer working under a services contract, confirmed by acceptance certificates and payment records.

items.status: Complaint lodged with the Working Group on Arbitrary Detention
items.text: The case has been referred to the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (WGAD), a treaty-based mechanism authorised to determine whether a detention — or the credible threat of one — is incompatible with international law.
items.focus: The WGAD assesses compliance with Articles 9 and 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights: the right to liberty and security of person, and the right to a fair trial. The central fact for assessment: the criminal charge was formulated in secret, without notifying the subject, two and a half years after the events in question took place.

items.status: Rule 39 refused. Full application being prepared.
items.text: The defence applied for Rule 39 interim measures — the Court's emergency procedure for temporarily blocking an extradition while the case is being examined. The application was refused. Russia withdrew from the Council of Europe in 2022 and is no longer a party to the Convention; Serbia, however, remains a Council of Europe member state and bears full Convention responsibility for what happens to Lagovsky as a consequence of extradition.
items.focus: The full application is built around several Convention articles used together. Article 3: a real risk of torture and inhuman treatment, given Russia's withdrawal from the UN Convention Against Torture and the documented threat of forced military mobilisation. Article 2: risk to life in an active combat zone. Article 8: the right to family life — Lagovsky's two minor children are in Serbia. Article 13: there is no effective domestic remedy, since the Minister of Justice's decision cannot be appealed. Article 6 is engaged not through the Serbian proceedings directly, but through the doctrine of 'flagrant denial of justice': extraditing someone to a judicial system that manifestly lacks independence is itself a Convention violation, regardless of what that system might then do.

items.text: On 21 April 2026 Lagovsky wrote to the UNHCR representation in Belgrade documenting the systemic failure of legal protection: the purely formalistic character of all asylum decisions, violations of Articles 3 and 8 of the ECHR, and the documented inaccessibility of justice in Russia. UNHCR replied that domestic remedies had not been exhausted, as the case was pending before the Administrative Court. UNHCR offered no substantive assessment of any of the arguments raised.
items.focus: The Serbian asylum procedure has run through every available instance up to the Asylum Commission — both levels refused, confining themselves to formal review. The only remaining barrier to extradition is the Administrative Court, which is now examining the challenge to the Commission's refusal. The statistical record in comparable cases gives no grounds for optimism. UNHCR's recommendation to wait effectively transfers responsibility for the outcome onto a procedure that has never ruled in favour of an applicant in a case of this kind.

summary: The international dimension is not a parallel version of the national proceedings — it is their external audit. Each of the four forums examines something different: Serbia examines a sovereign political decision; Interpol examines whether the wanted notice meets the organisation's own rules; WGAD examines whether the prosecution is arbitrary; the ECHR examines whether Serbia would bear Convention responsibility for the consequences of extradition. The refusal of Rule 39 interim measures does not prejudge the merits: Rule 39 is a rapid-response instrument operating under a high threshold, and the substantive application is assessed on entirely different grounds.
